papers.title_in_file: Is quantum advantage the right goal for quantum machine learning?
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v2 dated February 9, 2023 (perspective article); record id carries 2023, folder 2022.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Sec. I.C, Sec. II.A-B; Sec. III and IV not read in detail.
papers.what_it_is: A perspective article arguing that machine learning is a hard application for showing practical quantum advantage and that the focus on advantage should be debated.

assertions.value: The authors argue that, contrary to commercial expectations, machine learning may be one of the hardest applications for showing a practical quantum advantage, and give five reasons including strong classical baselines.
quotes: machine learning may turn out to be one of the hardest applications to show a practical quantum advantage for
machine learning is famous for notoriously powerful algorithms that set a challenging baseline for quantum algorithms
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' argument in a perspective article; no measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that showing quantum can beat classical machine learning may only be possible in highly abstract settings or on very small scales at this stage, and that focusing on advantage means focusing on a biased subset of models, datasets and theoretical approaches.
quotes: showing that quantum can beat classical machine learning may only be possible in highly abstract settings or on very small scales at this stage
Focusing on quantum advantage therefore means focusing only on a biased subset of models, datasets and theoretical approaches
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' argument in a perspective article.

assertions.value: The authors state that the learning regimes they want to understand are not observed at the small scales where few-qubit circuits can be simulated or run, so little can be said about quantum model behavior at realistic problem scale.
quotes: the learning regimes we are trying to understand are not observed on these small scales
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' argument in a perspective article.

papers.version_note: File is arXiv v2 (dated October 7, 2021), review.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Sec. IV.A (barren plateaus), Sec. VIII Outlook. The review is about 63 pages of body text; Secs. II, III, V, VI, VII not read in detail.
papers.what_it_is: A review of NISQ computational paradigms and algorithms, their limitations and advantages, and benchmarking and software tools.

assertions.value: The review states that at the time of writing there is no known demonstration of industrially relevant quantum advantage.
quotes: At the moment of documenting this review, there is no known demonstration of industrially relevant quantum advantage.
assertions.certainty_reason: Review authors' survey statement as of 2021; not a systematic search claim.
assertions.reader_inference: Time-scoped to the 2021 review; later work may differ.

assertions.value: The review states that dequantization efforts, first shown for recommendation systems, devise quantum-inspired classical algorithms nearly as fast as their quantum counterparts, and that such attempts have eliminated examples of speedup for some linear algebra problems.
quotes: devise quantum-inspired classical algorithms that are nearly as fast as their quantum counterparts
Such attempts have eliminated examples of speedup for some problems in linear algebra.
assertions.certainty_reason: Review's summary of other groups' results (Tang and others).

assertions.value: The review reports that, as shown by McClean et al. (2018), the expectation value of the gradient of the objective for randomly initialized parameterized quantum circuits decays exponentially to zero as a function of the number of qubits.
quotes: the expectation value of the gradient of the objective function corresponding to randomly initialized PQCs (RPQC) decays exponentially to zero as a function of the number of qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: Review reporting a result of McClean et al., 2018; the review does not prove it.

papers.title_in_file: Learning to Optimize Variational Quantum Circuits to Solve Combinatorial Problems
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v1 (Nov 2019) in AAAI 2020 format; record id carries 2019, folder 2020.
papers.what_it_is: Proposes two machine-learning approaches (reinforcement learning policy and kernel density estimation) for choosing QAOA variational parameters, tested by noiseless Qiskit Aer simulation on Max-Cut.

assertions.value: In noiseless Qiskit Aer simulation on a test set of 94 Max-Cut graph instances with a budget of 192 quantum circuit evaluations, the RL- and KDE-based approaches reduce the optimality gap by factors up to 30.15 compared with Nelder-Mead, with the paper stating the gap reduction factor is consistently larger than 1.
quotes: RL- and KDE-based approaches reduce the optimality gap by factors up to 30.15
compared with Nelder-Mead, and the gap reduction factor is consistently larger than 1
GTest contains 94 instances with varying number of vertices
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured on simulated QAOA, noiseless; no hardware.
assertions.reader_inference: The 30.15 factor is the maximum over graph classes and p in Table 2; other cells are as low as 1.05.

assertions.value: Training used one 8-vertex graph from each class and distribution (7 training instances), small enough to simulate classically, while the test set included larger instances.
quotes: we choose one representative graph instance of 8 vertices from each class and distribution, amounting to |GTrain| = 7 training instances
the training procedure is performed on small-sized problem instances that can be simulated on a classical computer
assertions.certainty_reason: Experimental design stated by the authors.

assertions.value: The results use Qiskit Aer to perform noiseless simulations of QAOA circuits.
quotes: We use Qiskit Aer to perform noiseless simulations of QAOA circuits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated experimental setup; the paper reports no hardware runs.

papers.title_in_file: Universal expressiveness of variational quantum classifiers and quantum kernels for support vector machines
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v2 dated February 10, 2023; record id carries 2023, folder 2022.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Results opening and gate-count paragraph, Discussion, start of Methods; the proofs in Methods were not checked line by line.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper showing that variational quantum classifiers and quantum-kernel SVMs can solve a classification problem based on k-Forrelation, which is PromiseBQP-complete.

assertions.value: The authors show that variational quantum classifiers and support vector machines with quantum kernels can solve a classification problem based on the k-Forrelation problem, known to be PromiseBQP-complete.
quotes: we show that variational quantum classifiers and support vector machines with quantum kernels can solve a classification problem based on the k-Forrelation problem
assertions.certainty_reason: Theoretical result in the paper; relies on the cited PromiseBQP-completeness of k-Forrelation.

assertions.value: The authors state their results imply that a feature map and a quantum kernel exist that make these models efficient solvers for any BQP problem.
quotes: there exists a feature map and a quantum kernel that make variational quantum classifiers and quantum kernel support vector machines efficient solvers for any BQP problem
assertions.certainty_reason: Implication drawn by the authors from their theorem; an existence statement about designable feature maps.
assertions.reader_inference: This is an existence claim for a designed feature map, not a claim that a trained model finds it.

assertions.value: The authors state that data embedding directly through their circuit results in shallower circuits of depth O(k) but is no longer a fixed ansatz; for the fixed ansatz they state O(kn^3) gates.
quotes: embedding the data directly through circuit (2) by applying a single (controlled) Z gate to the respective qubits, which is no longer a fixed ansatz, results in shallower circuits of depth O(k)
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated by the authors in their construction.

papers.title_in_file: A comprehensive review of Quantum Machine Learning: from NISQ to Fault Tolerance
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v2 dated 31 Mar 2024.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Introduction, Sec. 2.1.1 (objective function), Sec. 3.2 (dequantization), HHL caveats in Sec. 3.3; statistical learning theory sections not read in detail.
papers.what_it_is: A review of quantum machine learning concepts for NISQ and fault-tolerant devices, algorithms and statistical learning theory.

assertions.value: The review states that Tang introduced in 2019 a classical algorithm that dequantized the quantum recommendation systems algorithm with only polynomially slower runtime.
quotes: In 2019, Tang [121] introduced a classical algorithm that dequantized the quantum recommendation systems algorithm with only polynomially slower runtime
assertions.certainty_reason: Review reporting Tang's result.

assertions.value: The review states that classical algorithms for singular value transformation gave compelling evidence that, in the corresponding QRAM data structure input model, quantum SVT does not deliver exponential quantum speedups.
quotes: The results provided compelling evidence that, in the corresponding QRAM data structure input model, quantum SVT does not deliver exponential quantum speedups.
assertions.certainty_reason: Review characterizing a cited 2020 result.

assertions.value: The review states that learning any specific entry of the HHL solution by measurement will in general require repeating the algorithm roughly N times, negating the significant speedup.
quotes: Learning the value of any specific entry xi by measurement will, in general, require repeating the algorithm roughly N times, negating the significant speedup.
assertions.certainty_reason: Review restating a known caveat.

assertions.value: The review states that barren plateaus, where gradients vanish, are closely tied to the choice of the cost function, and that a poor choice can result in failure to locate a minimum by gradient descent.
quotes: Barren plateaus, where gradients vanish, are closely tied to the choice of the cost function. Therefore, a poor choice can result in a failure to locate a minimum of the objective function through gradient descent.
assertions.certainty_reason: Review statement.

papers.title_in_file: Variational Benchmarks for Quantum Many-Body Problems
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v2 dated Oct 2024 (document dated Sept. 12, 2024); record id 2024.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Secs. I-IV of the main text (V-score definition, Fig. 2 validation, hard problems, quantum advantage perspective, outlook); supplementary methods and per-method descriptions not read.
papers.what_it_is: Introduces the V-score, a metric of variational accuracy from variational energy and variance, with a curated dataset of variational calculations of many-body quantum systems.

assertions.value: The authors show in Fig. 2 that the V-score is a consistent estimator for the order of magnitude of the energy relative error across the Hamiltonians and variational methods they consider, and say this validates it at least for those Hamiltonians and techniques.
quotes: the V-score is a notably consistent and reliable estimator for the order of magnitude of the energy relative error
These results validate the V-score as an absolute performance metric for both classical and quantum variational algorithms, at least for the Hamiltonians and the techniques we consider in the paper.
assertions.certainty_reason: Measured against exact diagonalization and numerically exact QMC results, on the paper's dataset.

assertions.value: The authors report that frustrated geometries (triangular, kagome, pyrochlore, J1-J2 square) and fermionic models such as the Hubbard model are the most demanding for variational algorithms, and that for these hard problems the V-score correspondence predicts no better than one or two digits of accuracy on the energy.
quotes: frustrated geometries, such as triangular, kagome, pyrochlore, and the J1-J2 square lattice, as well as fermionic models, such as the Hubbard model, are the most demanding for variational algorithms
it predicts that we cannot expect an accuracy on the energy better than one or two digits
assertions.certainty_reason: Result over the authors' curated dataset of classical variational results.

assertions.value: The authors say it is unclear whether current noisy experimental quantum computing platforms can provide a solid and scalable advantage over classical ones, and infer from their V-scores that there is little room for quantum advantage in 1D geometries, where DMRG already achieves small V-scores.
quotes: it is unclear whether current noisy experimental quantum computing platforms can provide a solid and scalable advantage over classical ones
we can infer that there is little room for quantum advantage in 1D geometries
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' inference from their dataset of classical results.

papers.title_in_file: Automatic design of quantum feature maps
papers.version_note: File is arXiv v1 dated 26 May 2021.
papers.partial_detail: Abstract, Secs. 1-3, Sec. 4.1 (synthetic example), Sec. 4.3 (other use cases), Sec. 5; Sec. 4.2 skimmed.
papers.what_it_is: Proposes an NSGA-II multiobjective genetic algorithm that designs quantum feature map circuits for QSVM classification, tested in simulation.

assertions.value: The authors propose an NSGA-II multiobjective genetic algorithm that automatically generates ansatze for QSVM classification, maximizing accuracy and minimizing ansatz size.
quotes: This efficient method is based on NSGA-II multiobjective genetic algorithms which allow both maximize the accuracy and minimize the ansatz size.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' description of their method.

assertions.value: On a 150-point Moons synthetic non-linear dataset the 150 points are split 70% training and 30% test, the final circuit is reported at 1.0 accuracy in the Fig. 3 caption, and the authors validated the model with a set of 500 additional points generated by the same synthetic algorithm.
quotes: We validate the utility of the model using additional datapoints, a validation set, with 500 points generated by the same synthetic algorithm.
The 150 datapoints are scaled between [-1,+1] as a preprocessing step, and randomly split into a training (70%) and test (30%) sets.
assertions.certainty_reason: One synthetic dataset, simulation, single reported run.

assertions.value: The authors report that two of the generated circuits for the three benchmark problems are uncorrelated and have no CNOT gates, the third has just one entangler gate, and that such structures admit an efficient classical simulation.
quotes: two of the circuits are uncorrelated and have no CNOT gates, while the third one, for multiclass drug classification, has just one entangler gate
admit an efficient classical simulation which constitutes in itself a type of quantum-inspired machine-learning technique
assertions.certainty_reason: Observed structure of circuits found on three benchmark datasets in simulation.
assertions.reader_inference: This bears on whether the paper's QSVM advantage claim over classical classifiers is quantum at all; the authors themselves note the circuits are classically simulable.
